subtopics.title: Function & Class Templates
subtopics.subtitle: Writing one definition for many types: function templates, overloading and class templates

concepts.text: Why Generic Programming

Generic programming means writing an algorithm or a data structure once, in terms of a type that is filled in later, instead of copying the same code for int, double, string and so on. In C++ this is done with templates: a template is a blueprint from which the compiler generates (instantiates) a concrete function or class for each type actually used. The generated code is type-checked and as fast as hand-written code, unlike C macros (no type checking) or void* tricks (no safety). The Standard Template Library is built entirely on this idea.
Function Templates
Rules of function templates:
items: Syntax: template <typename T> (or template <class T>) immediately before the function; typename and class mean exactly the same thing here.
Template argument deduction: the compiler works out T from the argument types at the call; every use of T must deduce to the same type, otherwise the call is an error.
Explicit arguments: maxOf<double>(4, 6.5) forces T; required when T appears only in the return type or cannot be deduced.
Multiple parameters: template <typename T, typename U> lets each argument have its own type; parameters given explicitly are matched left to right, the rest are deduced.
Each distinct set of template arguments produces a separate copy of the function (an instantiation) at compile time; the template itself generates no code until used.

concepts.text: Overloading Function Templates

A function template can be overloaded with other templates and with ordinary (non-template) functions of the same name. Overload resolution then follows a fixed preference: an ordinary function that matches the arguments exactly is chosen over any template; otherwise the template that fits with no conversion is chosen; if two templates both fit, the more specialised one (for example T* over T) wins; a non-template that needs a conversion loses to a template that matches exactly, because deduction can always produce an exact match.
Class Templates
Points about class templates:
items: Syntax: template <class T> class Name { ... };  T can be used for data members, member function parameters and return types.
Instantiation is always explicit for classes: Stack<int> s; the compiler cannot deduce T from a constructor call in C++11 (that arrived only in C++17).
Member functions defined outside the class need the full header again: template <class T> void Stack<T>::push(T x) { ... }. The class name is Stack<T>, not Stack.
Because the compiler must see the template to instantiate it, template definitions normally live in the header file, not in a separate .cpp.
Non-type parameters (template <class T, int N>) accept constant expressions such as array sizes; default template arguments (int N = 10) work like default function arguments.
Stack<int> and Stack<double> are unrelated classes: they share no static members and cannot be assigned to each other.

concepts.text: Specialisation in outline: a template can be given a special version for one particular type when the general code would be wrong or slow for it, written as template <> class Stack<bool> { ... } (explicit specialisation) or template <class T> class Stack<T*> { ... } (partial specialisation, classes only). Function templates allow full specialisation only; in practice an ordinary overload is preferred. Specialisation is what lets STL containers store bool or pointers efficiently.

MCQs often test the exact spelling of template headers (template <typename T>, template <class T> Stack<T>::push), what T is deduced as for a given call, and which overload is picked when a template and a non-template both apply. Trace the argument types carefully: an int literal is int, 2.5 is double, 'a' is char and "text" is const char*.
Going Deeper: Deduction, Specialisation and Instantiation

Template argument deduction compares each function parameter type P with the type A of the matching argument and solves for the template parameters. For a by-value parameter T the argument first decays: an array becomes a pointer to its first element, a function becomes a function pointer, and top-level const is dropped, because the function works on a copy. For a reference parameter T& or const T& nothing decays, so T can become an array type such as int[5]. Deduction does not apply the ordinary implicit conversions such as int to double (only small adjustments such as adding const are allowed) and never looks at the return type, which is why maxOf(3, 4.5) fails and why a parameter used only in the return type must be written explicitly.

Output (8-byte double and pointer, ASCII):
8 32
4 A 3.5

byValue(d)       T = double*, the array decayed: sizeof = 8
byRef(d)         T = double[4], no decay: 4 x 8 = 32
as<int>(d[3])    R = int given, T = double deduced: 4.5 -> 4
as<char>(65)     R = char: 65 is 'A', printed as a character
as<double>(7)/2  R = double: 7.0 / 2 = 3.5, not integer division

An explicit specialisation such as template <> void f<char>(char) is not a new overload: it only supplies a different body for one instantiation of an existing primary template. Overload resolution therefore works in two steps. First the compiler compares the ordinary functions and the primary templates, with their deduced arguments, and picks the best; an ordinary function wins a tie with a template, and between two templates the more specialised one wins. Only if the winner is a primary template does the compiler check whether that particular instantiation has an explicit specialisation, and use its body if it has.

Output: spec-char ordinary primary primary primary

f('x')       f(int) needs a char -> int promotion; the template gives
             T = char exactly, so the template wins, and f<char>
             has an explicit specialisation: spec-char
f(7)         f(int) and f<int> are both exact: the ordinary one wins
f(7L)        only the template is exact (T = long): primary
f<>(7)       empty <> allows templates only: f<int>, not specialised
f<int>('x')  T fixed as int, 'x' converted to 120: primary

Each distinct, complete list of template arguments names a different specialisation: default arguments are filled in first, so Row<> and Row<int, 3> are the same class while Row<int, 4> is another one with its own static members. Only what is used gets instantiated: a member function of Stack<int> is compiled only if it is called, so a class template can hold a type that lacks an operator needed by an uncalled member. The declaration template class Stack<int>; (an explicit instantiation) forces every member to be generated in that file, which lets template code stay in a .cpp file for a fixed set of types. Because non-type arguments are compile-time constants, a class template can even recurse on them, with an explicit specialisation as the base case.

concepts.latex: F\langle N\rangle = N \cdot F\langle N-1\rangle,\quad F\langle 0\rangle = 1
concepts.plainText: F<N>::value = N x F<N-1>::value, with the explicit specialisation F<0>::value = 1 as the base case; e.g. F<4> = 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 x 1 = 24, computed entirely by the compiler

concepts.text: Common mistakes with templates:
items: Naming a dependent type without typename: inside template <class C>, C::const_iterator it; does not compile; write typename C::const_iterator it;.
Giving a class template parameter a default and a later parameter none: template <class T = int, class U> class P; is ill-formed.
Using a run-time variable as a non-type argument: int n = 8; Buf<n> b; fails, while const int k = 8; Buf<k> b; is fine.
An out-of-class member definition must match its declaration exactly, including const: template <class T> T Box<T>::get() const { return v; }.
An explicit specialisation must be declared before the first use that would implicitly instantiate the same template arguments; place it right after the primary template.
Expecting a function template specialisation to beat an ordinary overload: specialisations never take part in overload resolution, so an ordinary overload is usually the clearer choice.

concepts.text: To predict which function a call runs: (1) deduce T for every candidate template from the argument types, allowing no conversions; (2) rank the ordinary functions and templates, letting an ordinary function win a tie and the more specialised template win between templates; (3) only then swap in an explicit specialisation if the winning template has one. For class templates, fill in default arguments before deciding whether two names are the same type. Under C++17, Box b(2.5); deduces Box<double> from the constructor argument.

formulas.plainText: instantiations = number of distinct <T> argument sets actually used (zero if never called)
Stack<T, N> data storage = N × sizeof(T) bytes (plus the int top)
Overload preference: non-template exact match > template exact match > non-template needing conversion

notes.text: When an ordinary function and a function template both match a call exactly, the ordinary function is chosen. The template only wins when the ordinary function would need a conversion (e.g. print('a') with print(int) and template print(T) calls the template with T = char).

maxOf(3, 4.5) with template <typename T> T maxOf(T, T) is a compile error, not a promotion: deduction gives T = int from the first argument and T = double from the second. Fix it with maxOf<double>(3, 4.5) or two type parameters.

Outside the class, a member of a class template is defined as template <class T> ReturnType ClassName<T>::member(...) { ... }. Forgetting the <T> after the class name, or the template <class T> header, is the classic syntax slip.

formulas.title: Template instantiation
formulas.plainText: instantiations = number of distinct <T> argument sets used
formulas.description: The compiler generates one concrete function or class per distinct set of template arguments; an unused template produces no code at all.

formulas.title: Stack<T, N> storage
formulas.plainText: storage of T data[N] = N × sizeof(T) bytes
formulas.description: A class template with a non-type parameter N holding T data[N] needs N × sizeof(T) bytes for its array, e.g. Stack<double, 5> needs 40 bytes plus the top index.

formulas.title: Overload preference
formulas.plainText: non-template exact match > template exact match > match needing a conversion
formulas.description: The order in which overload resolution ranks candidates when a call could go to an ordinary function or to a function template.

flashcards.front: Is there any difference between template <typename T> and template <class T>?
flashcards.back: No. Both declare a type parameter T; typename and class are interchangeable in a template parameter list.

flashcards.front: How is a member function of class template Stack<T> defined outside the class body?
flashcards.back: Repeat the header and qualify with the template name: template <class T> void Stack<T>::push(T x) { ... }.

flashcards.front: Given void f(int) and template <typename T> void f(T), which is called by f(10) and by f(2.5)?
flashcards.back: f(10) calls the non-template f(int) because it matches exactly; f(2.5) calls the template with T = double because f(int) would need a conversion.

flashcards.front: What is a non-type template parameter?
flashcards.back: A template parameter that is a constant value rather than a type, e.g. template <class T, int N> class Array; N must be a compile-time constant such as an array size.

questions.explanation: half(7) deduces T = int so 7 / 2 is integer division giving 3; half<double>(7) forces T = double, 7 is converted to 7.0 and 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5.

questions.questionText: Class template Stack declares a member void push(T x); inside template <class T> class Stack { ... };. Which is the correct way to define push outside the class?
questions.explanation: An out-of-class member definition of a class template must repeat the template header and qualify the member with the template-id Stack<T>; without the header T is undeclared, and without <T> the compiler does not know which class is meant.

questions.questionText: A program defines template <typename T> T cube(T x) { return x * x * x; } but never calls cube or uses it in any other way. What code does the compiler generate from this template?
options: One version for every built-in arithmetic type, ready for later calls
None: code is generated only for the template arguments the program actually uses
One generic version working on void* that is reused for all types
A single copy that is linked into the program and specialised at run time
questions.explanation: A template is only a blueprint. The compiler instantiates a concrete function for a type only when the program uses the template with that type, so an unused template produces no code (it is merely checked for syntax).

questions.questionText: For the function template template <class T> T sq(T x) { return x * x; }, which types can be used as T?
options: Only class types, because the keyword class is used
Only built-in types such as int and double
Any type for which the operations used in the body (copying and *) are valid, such as int, double or a class that overloads *
questions.explanation: In a template parameter list, class means the same as typename: T may be any type, built-in or user-defined. The only requirement is that the body compiles for that type, here that T can be copied and multiplied.

options: Compile error: + cannot be applied when T is string
questions.explanation: Three instantiations are made: T = int gives 4 + 4 = 8; T = double gives 3.0, which cout prints as 3; T = string uses the string + operator (concatenation), so ab followed by ab gives abab.
swapT takes its parameters by reference, so the originals are exchanged. swapT(x, y) uses T = int and swapT(p, q) uses T = char, giving x = 2, y = 1, p = 'q', q = 'p', printed as 21qp.
succ('A') deduces T = char: 'A' + 1 is computed as the int 66 but is converted back to char on return, so cout prints the character B. succ(65) deduces T = int and prints 66.

questions.questionText: Given template <typename T> void f(T a, T b) { }, which of these calls compiles?
questions.explanation: In the first three calls deduction gets two different types for T (int and long, char and int, float and double) and fails, because deduction does not convert one argument to the type of the other. With T given explicitly as double nothing is deduced, and 1 and 2.5f are simply converted to double.
For the by-value parameter the array decays, so T = int* and sizeof(x) = 8. For the reference parameter there is no decay, T = int[10] and sizeof(x) = 10 x 4 = 40 bytes.
In add(5, 2.7), T = int and U = double; 5 + 2.7 = 7.7 is converted to the return type int, giving 7. In add(2.7, 5), T = double, so 7.7 is returned unchanged.

questions.questionText: Given template <typename T> T zero() { return T(); }, which statement compiles?
questions.explanation: T appears only in the return type, and the type of the variable being initialised is not used for deduction, so T must be given explicitly: zero<int>() returns int(), which is 0. The other forms either leave T undeduced or are not valid syntax.

Explicit arguments fill R, T, U from the left and the rest are deduced. mul<int>(2.5, 3): 2.5 x 3 = 7.5 returned as int, 7. mul<double, int>(2.5, 3): T = int converts 2.5 to 2, so 2 x 3 = 6. mul<double>(2.5, 3): T = double, giving 7.5.

questions.questionText: Which line correctly begins an explicit (full) specialisation of template <typename T> void show(T x) for T = const char*?
options: template <> void show<const char*>(const char* x)
template <typename T> void show<const char*>(T x)
specialize <const char*> void show(const char* x)
questions.explanation: An explicit specialisation starts with an empty parameter list, template <>, followed by the function with the template argument written after its name. Function templates cannot be partially specialised, template <> may not be omitted, and C++ has no specialize keyword.

Deduction gives T = int, double, float and char for the four calls. Only kind(1.0) produces the specialised instantiation kind<double>; 1.0f makes T = float, which uses the general version, so the output is GDGG.

questions.questionText: A program defines template <class T> class Box { ... }; and after it template <> class Box<bool> { ... };. Which statement is correct?
options: Box<bool> automatically inherits every member of the primary template and may only add new ones
The specialisation is used for bool and also for every type that converts to bool, such as int
Box<bool> is a completely separate class definition used whenever Box<bool> is named; its members need not match the primary template
The specialisation must appear before the primary template in the source
questions.explanation: A full specialisation replaces the whole class for exactly that argument list; nothing is inherited from the primary template, so Box<bool> may have entirely different members. It applies only to Box<bool>, and it must come after the primary template has been declared.
pi is a Printer<int>, so print(true) converts true to the int 1 and prints [1]. pb uses the specialisation Printer<bool>: true prints [yes], and 0 is converted to false and prints [no].

options: Compile error: the call is ambiguous
questions.explanation: f<int*>(int*) is a specialisation of the first template (T = int* turns f(T) into f(int*)). Overload resolution compares only the primary templates: f(T) with T = int* and f(T*) with T = int are both exact, and the more specialised f(T*) wins, so 2 is printed; the specialisation of the losing template is never used.

questions.questionText: A call matches an ordinary (non-template) function and a function template equally well, with no conversion needed for either. Which one does the compiler call?
options: The function template, because a template is more general
Neither: the call is ambiguous and does not compile
Whichever of the two is declared first in the file
questions.explanation: When the conversion sequences are equally good, the tie-breaker rule prefers a non-template function over a function generated from a template. For example, with void f(int) and template <class T> void f(T), the call f(10) runs f(int).

show(2.0): show(double) and show<double> are both exact, so the ordinary function wins (d). show(2) and show(2.0f): the template gives T = int or float exactly, which beats the conversion to double (T, T). show<>(2.0): the empty <> restricts the call to templates, so T is printed.

g(n): only g(T) fits (A). g(&n): g(T*) with T = int matches int* exactly, while g(const T*) needs an int* to const int* conversion, and g(T*) is more specialised than g(T) (B). g(&c): all three match const int* exactly and g(const T*) is the most specialised (C).

questions.questionText: Which description of a class template is correct?
options: A class that has only pure virtual functions and cannot be instantiated
A pattern with parameters from which the compiler generates a separate class for each set of template arguments used
A class from which every other class in the program must be derived
A class whose objects can be created only with new
questions.explanation: A class template such as template <class T> class Stack is a blueprint; Stack<int> and Stack<double> are two distinct classes generated from it. The first option describes an abstract class, not a template.

questions.questionText: Given template <class T> class Pair { T first, second; };, which statement correctly creates an object of Pair holding int values?
questions.explanation: The template arguments are written in angle brackets directly after the template name: Pair<int> p;. Pair<int> is then used exactly like an ordinary class name.
Duo<int> stores ints, so sum() returns 3 + 4 = 7. Duo<double> stores doubles, so sum() returns 1.5 + 2.25 = 3.75; cout prints 7 without a decimal point.
Each instantiation is a separate class with its own static member. Counter<int>::count is increased by a, b and d (3) and Counter<double>::count only by c (1).

get is declared as a const member function, so its out-of-class definition must also say const: template <class T> T Box<T>::get() const { return v; }. Without const the definition matches no member declared in Box<T>.

questions.questionText: Why are the member function definitions of a class template normally written in the header file along with the class, instead of in a separately compiled .cpp file?
options: The compiler must see the full definitions wherever a new specialisation such as Stack<int> is used, so that it can generate the code there
C++ does not allow the keyword template to appear in a .cpp file
Class template members are processed by the preprocessor, which reads only header files
Placing them in the header makes every member function virtual
questions.explanation: Code for Stack<int>::push is generated only where the compiler sees both the use and the template definition. If the definitions sit in another .cpp file, the calls compile but linking fails with undefined references, unless that file explicitly instantiates the needed types.
With N = 3, pos cycles 0, 1, 2, 0, 1. The puts store 10 in d[0], 20 in d[1], 30 in d[2], then 40 overwrites d[0] and 50 overwrites d[1], so the array holds 40 50 30.

questions.questionText: Under C++17, what is the type of b after the declaration Box b(2.5); given template <class T> struct Box { T v; Box(T x) : v(x) {} };?
options: It does not compile: the template argument must be written, as in Box<double> b(2.5);
questions.explanation: C++17 added class template argument deduction: the constructor argument 2.5 is a double, so T = double and b is a Box<double>. Before C++17 the template argument had to be written explicitly.

C::const_iterator depends on the template parameter C, and the compiler assumes such a qualified name is not a type unless it is preceded by typename. Writing typename C::const_iterator it declares it as an iterator variable.

questions.questionText: In template <class T, int N> class Array { T a[N]; };, what kind of template parameter is N?
options: A type parameter, so Array<int, double> is valid
A default argument that the constructor receives at run time
A run-time variable that can change after an object is created
A non-type parameter: its argument must be a compile-time constant of type int, as in Array<char, 16>
questions.explanation: N is a non-type (value) template parameter. Its argument must be a constant expression, because it becomes part of the type: Array<char, 16> and Array<char, 32> are different classes.
power<3>(2) multiplies 2 three times: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. In power<0>(5) the loop runs zero times, so r keeps its starting value 1.

A non-type template argument must be a constant expression. k is a const int initialised with a constant and sizeof(int) is known at compile time, but n is an ordinary variable, so Buf<n> is rejected.
size() returns the non-type argument N = 5. The member array T a[N] occupies N x sizeof(T) bytes: 5 x 8 = 40 for double and 5 x 1 = 5 for char.

options: Compile error: the recursion in Fact never ends
questions.explanation: Fact<5> needs Fact<4>, down to Fact<0>, which is the explicit specialisation with value 1 and stops the recursion. The compiler computes 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 x 1 = 120, and Fact<0>::value is 1.
Missing arguments take their defaults. Row<> is Row<int, 3>: 3 x 4 = 12 bytes. Row<char> is Row<char, 3>: 3 x 1 = 3 bytes. Row<double, 2> overrides both: 2 x 8 = 16 bytes.

questions.questionText: Which class template declaration does NOT compile?
options: template <class T, class U = T> class P;
template <class T = int, class U> class P;
template <class T, int N = 10> class P;
template <class T = char, int N = 5> class P;
questions.explanation: As with default function arguments, once a class template parameter has a default, every parameter after it must have one too, so T = int followed by a plain U is ill-formed. A default may refer to an earlier parameter, as in U = T.

avg(3.0, 4.0): R takes its default int, so 3.5 is returned as 3. avg<double>(3.0, 4.0): R = double, giving 3.5. avg<double>(3, 4): T is deduced as int, so (3 + 4) / 2 is integer division = 3, returned as 3.0 and printed as 3.

questions.questionText: Which template header does NOT compile when it is followed by struct X { };?
questions.explanation: Each template parameter must have a distinct name, so declaring T twice is an error. Mixing typename and class, or type and non-type parameters, is allowed.

questions.questionText: Compared with the function-like macro #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b)), what is an advantage of the function template template <class T> T maxOf(T a, T b)?
options: The template is expanded by the preprocessor, so it never adds a function call
The template can also be used in C programs
The template's arguments are type-checked and each argument expression is evaluated exactly once
The template accepts two arguments of different types, such as maxOf(3, 4.5), without any extra code
questions.explanation: A template is compiled like a real function: arguments are type-checked and evaluated once, so maxOf(i++, j) increments i only once. Templates are handled by the compiler, not the preprocessor, do not exist in C, and maxOf(3, 4.5) fails deduction.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing function templates with function-like macros is NOT correct?
options: A template obeys scope and namespace rules, while a macro name is replaced everywhere after its #define
Both are expanded by the preprocessor before the compiler proper sees the code
A template can be given a specialised version for one particular type
An argument such as i++ passed to a template is evaluated only once
questions.explanation: Only macros are handled by the preprocessor, as plain text substitution; templates are instantiated by the compiler, with full type checking. The other three statements are true.

The macro becomes ((9) > (2.5) ? (9) : (2.5)) / 2; a conditional with int and double operands has type double, so 9.0 / 2 = 4.5. maxT<int> converts 2.5 to 2 and returns the int 9, so 9 / 2 is integer division = 4.

questions.questionText: When is a function template instantiated for a particular type such as int?
options: At compile time, when the compiler meets a use (such as a call) that needs that type
At link time, when the object files are combined
At run time, the first time the function is called
questions.explanation: Instantiation is done by the compiler: a use such as maxOf(3, 7) makes it generate and type-check maxOf<int>. Nothing about templates happens at run time.

One function is generated per distinct deduced type, not per call: neg<int> (for 2, 3 and 5), neg<double>, neg<float> and neg<char>, which makes 4. 2.0f is a float and 'a' is a char, so neither reuses another instantiation.

Each instantiation has its own static n. counter<int> is called with 1, 2 and then 4, so it returns 3; counter<double> is called with 3.0 and then 5.0, so it returns 2; counter<char> is new and returns 1.

options: Compile error in inc(), because S has no ++ operator
Compile error in show(), because S cannot be printed with <<
It compiles, but the program crashes when w is created
questions.explanation: A member function of a class template is instantiated only if it is used. W<S> creates the class with its data member, but inc() and show() are never called, so their bodies are never compiled for S.

The template body is checked for a type only when it is instantiated with it. big, big and big are fine, but instantiating big

fails because a > b has no meaning for struct P, which defines no > operator.

Default arguments are filled in first: V<int> is V<int, 4>, the same type as b, and V<double> is V<double, 4>, the same type as e. The distinct classes are V<int, 4>, V<int, 8> and V<double, 4>, which makes 3.

questions.questionText: Stack is a class template. What does the statement template class Stack<int>; do?
options: It declares a new, empty class named Stack<int> that replaces the template's members
It creates a global object of type Stack<int>
It explicitly instantiates Stack<int>: the definitions of all its member functions are generated in this file even if none is called
It forbids Stack from being used with any type other than int
questions.explanation: template class Stack<int>; is an explicit instantiation definition. It makes the compiler generate every member of Stack<int> in that translation unit, which is how template definitions can be kept in a .cpp file for a known set of types.

subtopics.title: Standard Template Library (STL)
subtopics.subtitle: Containers, iterators and algorithms: the ready-made generic toolkit of C++

concepts.text: What the STL Is

The Standard Template Library is the part of the C++ standard library that provides generic data structures and algorithms as templates. It has three main components: containers (objects that store collections of elements), algorithms (functions such as sort or find that operate on ranges of elements) and iterators (pointer-like objects that connect the two by pointing at elements inside a container). Two supporting pieces complete the picture: function objects (functors, e.g. greater<int>) that customise what an algorithm does, and allocators that manage container memory behind the scenes. Because algorithms talk to containers only through iterators, any algorithm works with any container that offers the right kind of iterator.
Containers
Sequence containers keep elements in the order you insert them:
items: vector (<vector>): dynamic array in contiguous memory; O(1) index access and push_back at the end (amortised); insertion in the middle shifts elements; grows automatically.
deque (<deque>): double-ended queue; O(1) push/pop at both ends and indexed access; elements in several chunks, not one contiguous block.
list (<list>): doubly linked list; O(1) insert/erase anywhere given an iterator; no indexing with [] and no random access.
array (<array>, C++11): fixed-size array wrapper, size is a template argument (array<int, 5>); knows its size, supports iterators.
forward_list (<forward_list>, C++11): singly linked list; forward traversal only, smallest overhead.

concepts.text: Associative and unordered containers are keyed and searched, not indexed by position:
items: set / multiset (<set>): sorted unique keys / sorted keys with duplicates allowed; implemented as balanced binary search trees (red-black), so insert, erase and find are O(log n).
map / multimap (<map>): sorted key-value pairs; map keys unique, multimap allows repeated keys; map supports m[key] which inserts a default value if the key is absent.
unordered_set, unordered_multiset, unordered_map, unordered_multimap (C++11): hash tables; average O(1) lookup, no ordering of elements.
Iterating a set or map visits elements in ascending key order (by operator< or a supplied comparator); iterating an unordered container gives no guaranteed order.

concepts.text: Container adapters wrap another container to give a restricted interface (no iterators):
items: stack (<stack>): LIFO; push, pop, top, empty, size; built on deque by default.
queue (<queue>): FIFO; push at back, pop from front, front, back; built on deque by default.
priority_queue (<queue>): always pops the largest element (max-heap by default, a comparator such as greater<int> gives a min-heap); built on vector by default.

rows: O(1) amortised at end; O(n) in the middle
O(1) at both ends; O(n) in the middle

concepts.text: Iterators
An iterator behaves like a pointer to an element: *it reads the element, ++it moves on, and it != end() tests for the end. Five categories, each adding capability to the previous:
items: Input iterator: read forward once, single pass (e.g. istream_iterator).
Output iterator: write forward once, single pass (e.g. ostream_iterator, back_inserter).
Forward iterator: read/write, multi-pass, ++ only (forward_list, unordered containers).
Bidirectional iterator: adds -- (list, set, map, multiset, multimap).
Random-access iterator: adds it + n, it - n, it[n], comparison with < (vector, deque, array, plain pointers).

Every container provides begin() and end(); end() points one past the last element, so [begin, end) is a half-open range. Constant versions are cbegin()/cend(); reverse iterators rbegin()/rend() traverse backwards.

MCQs usually ask which container fits a description (dynamic array, LIFO, sorted unique keys, key-value pairs), which header an algorithm needs, and the output of short vector, map or sort programs.
Going Deeper: Using STL Containers Correctly

A vector keeps its size() elements inside one block that has room for capacity() elements. When push_back finds size() equal to capacity(), it allocates a larger block, moves every existing element across, constructs the new element there and frees the old block, which is why every iterator into the vector becomes invalid at that moment. Implementations grow the capacity geometrically (typically by a factor of 1.5 or 2) rather than by a fixed amount, so reallocations become rarer as the vector grows. reserve(n) allocates room for at least n elements without changing size(), and shrink_to_fit() asks the vector to give back unused space.

subtopics.title: Exception Handling
subtopics.subtitle: try, throw and catch: reporting and recovering from run-time errors without error codes

concepts.text: Why Exceptions

In C, a function reports failure through a return value (-1, NULL, an errno code) that the caller must remember to test, and the test is easily forgotten or awkward when the function already returns a value (what does divide() return when b is 0?). Exception handling separates error detection from error handling: the function that detects the problem throws an exception object, execution leaves that function immediately, and control is transferred to the nearest enclosing handler that can deal with it, possibly many calls up the stack. Errors cannot be silently ignored, the normal code path stays clean, and constructors, which return nothing, get a way to report failure.
try, throw and catch
Mechanics of the three keywords:
items: try { ... } encloses the code that may fail; one or more catch blocks must follow it immediately.
throw expression; creates a copy of the value (any type: int, const char*, a class object) and starts the search for a handler; the rest of the try block is skipped.
catch (Type name) { ... } handles an exception whose type matches; after the handler finishes, execution continues after the last catch block, not back at the throw point.

Stack unwinding: as control leaves each function between the throw and the handler, local objects are destroyed (their destructors run) exactly as on a normal return; heap memory freed only in skipped code leaks.
If the try block completes without throwing, all its catch blocks are skipped.

concepts.text: Multiple Handlers, Matching Order, Rethrow
Several catch blocks may follow one try; they are tested in the order written and the first match wins:
items: Matching is by type: an int handler does not catch a double (no arithmetic conversions), but a handler for a base class catches a derived-class object, and a pointer/reference to base catches derived.

Therefore write derived-class handlers before base-class handlers; a catch (exception&) placed first would swallow every std exception and the later specific handlers would be unreachable (compilers warn).
Catch by reference (catch (const T &e)) to avoid copying and to keep the dynamic type; catching a derived object by base value slices it.
catch (...) catches every type; it must be last and it cannot access the exception object.
throw; (empty throw) inside a handler rethrows the current exception object unchanged to an outer try; throw e; would throw a copy of the static type instead.
A try block can be nested inside another try or inside a handler; an exception not handled by the inner block propagates to the outer one.

concepts.text: Exceptions with Arguments and Nested try

Throwing a class object is the normal style because the object can carry arguments describing the error (the bad value, a message, a code) through its constructor, and because a hierarchy of exception classes lets callers choose how specific to be. Nested try blocks let an inner handler do local clean-up and then rethrow to an outer handler that reports to the user; an inner try without a matching handler simply passes the exception outward, and a throw inside a catch block is itself handled by the enclosing try, never by a sibling catch of the same try.
Exception Specifications, Uncaught and Unexpected
How a function advertises what it may throw, and what happens when nothing catches an exception:
items: Dynamic exception specification (pre-C++11): void f() throw(int, char); promised only those types, and void f() throw(); promised none. Violating it called std::unexpected(), which by default called std::terminate(); set_unexpected() could install another handler. Deprecated in C++11, removed in C++17.

noexcept (C++11): void f() noexcept; declares that f does not throw; if it does anyway, std::terminate() is called at once with no unwinding. noexcept(expr) is also a compile-time operator that yields true if expr cannot throw.

Uncaught exception: if the handler search reaches main() without a match, std::terminate() is called, which by default calls abort(); no destructors of main's locals are guaranteed to run. set_terminate(handler) installs a custom terminate handler that must not return.
Exceptions thrown by destructors during unwinding (a second active exception) also lead to terminate(), so destructors should not throw.

concepts.text: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation) is the idiom that makes exceptions safe: a resource such as heap memory, a file or a lock is owned by a local object whose constructor acquires it and whose destructor releases it. Because stack unwinding runs destructors of every local object between the throw and the handler, the resource is released automatically whether the function ends normally or by exception. This is why smart pointers, fstream and lock_guard are preferred to raw new/delete and fopen/fclose in C++ code that may throw.
Going Deeper: What Happens After throw

When a throw expression runs, its operand is copied (or moved) into a special exception object whose type is the static type of the expression, so throwing a Base& that refers to a Derived object throws a Base. The run-time system then searches outward for a handler: first the catch clauses of the innermost enclosing try block, then those of the try blocks in each calling function in turn. Before the chosen handler runs, every automatic object created since that try block was entered is destroyed in reverse order of construction, innermost function first; this is stack unwinding. The exception object itself lives until the last handler dealing with it exits without rethrowing.

Output: +a +b +c -c -b caught 42 end -a

line 12  main calls middle(); on line 9 it constructs b: +b and calls inner()
line 8   inner() constructs c: +c, then throws 42
unwind   inner() is left early, c is destroyed: -c
unwind   middle() is left early, "never" is skipped, b is destroyed: -b
line 13  catch (int e) in main receives 42: caught 42
line 14  execution resumes after the handler: end
exit     main returns and a is destroyed last: -a

An object counts as constructed only when its constructor finishes. If a constructor throws, the destructor of that object is not called, but every base-class subobject and data member that was already fully constructed is destroyed in reverse order, and memory obtained by new for the object is freed automatically. Raw resources acquired inside the constructor body are not released, which is another reason to hold them in members such as vector or unique_ptr. Destructors are implicitly noexcept since C++11, so a throw that escapes a destructor calls std::terminate(), and when no handler exists at all it is implementation-defined whether any unwinding happens before terminate().

items: Writing catch (Base &) before catch (Derived &): the derived handler can never run.
Catching class exceptions by value: the copy is sliced and a virtual what() reports the base version.
Rethrowing with throw e; instead of throw;: it throws a copy of the static type, not the original object.
Expecting catch (int) to take a char, a short or a double: exception matching applies no arithmetic conversions.
Expecting the statements after the throw, or later in the try block, to run once the handler finishes.
Releasing resources with delete or fclose after code that may throw: unwinding skips them, so use RAII objects.
Letting an exception escape a destructor or a noexcept function: std::terminate() is called.

concepts.text: Library code describes its behaviour under exceptions with three levels of guarantee. The basic guarantee promises no leaks and objects left in a valid but unspecified state; the strong guarantee promises that an operation either succeeds completely or has no effect at all, as vector::push_back does; the no-throw guarantee promises that the operation never throws, which is exactly what noexcept declares. This is why noexcept matters in practice: when a vector reallocates, it moves its elements only if the element type's move constructor is noexcept (or the type cannot be copied), otherwise it copies them so that push_back can keep its strong guarantee.

To trace an exception question: (1) print everything up to the throw; (2) skip the rest of the try block and of every function being left; (3) run the destructors of their local objects, newest first and innermost function first; (4) pick the first handler, in written order, whose type matches; (5) continue after that try-catch, or keep unwinding if the handler rethrows.

formulas.plainText: throw → stack unwinding (destructors run) → first catch whose type matches, tested in written order
uncaught exception → std::terminate() → abort() (program ends abnormally)
throw() of C++03 is replaced by noexcept in C++11; throwing from a noexcept function calls terminate()

notes.text: Order of handlers: most specific (derived) first, base class later, catch (...) last. Type matching is exact apart from derived-to-base and pointer conversions: throw 3.5 is not caught by catch (int), and throw 'a' is not caught by catch (int) either.

After a handler runs, execution continues after the whole try-catch construct, never at the statement following the throw. Any cout in the try block after the throwing call is skipped, which is the basis of most output-prediction questions on this topic.

throw; (empty) rethrows the current exception and is legal only inside a catch block; anywhere else it calls terminate(). throw e; from a handler throws a copy, which slices a derived object caught by base value.

Three ways a program reaches std::terminate(): an exception with no matching handler, an exception escaping a noexcept function, and a second exception thrown while unwinding (e.g. from a destructor). std::unexpected() belongs to the old throw(...) specifications and is legacy.

formulas.title: Handler search
formulas.plainText: throw → stack unwinding → first matching catch in written order
formulas.description: Handlers of a try block are tested top to bottom and the first whose type matches (exactly or by derived-to-base conversion) runs; the rest are skipped.

formulas.title: Uncaught exception
formulas.plainText: uncaught exception → std::terminate() → abort()
formulas.description: When the search leaves main() without a match, terminate() is called; set_terminate() can replace the default handler but the program still cannot resume.

formulas.title: Exception specifications
formulas.plainText: throw() specification (C++03) replaced by noexcept (C++11)
formulas.description: Both declare a non-throwing function; the old dynamic specifications throw(T1, T2) that called unexpected() on violation were deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17.

flashcards.front: Why should a catch block for a derived exception class come before one for its base class?
flashcards.back: Handlers are tried in written order and a base-class handler also matches derived objects, so a base handler placed first would catch everything and make the derived handler unreachable.
The process, between a throw and its handler, of leaving each intermediate function and destroying its local objects (running their destructors) as if those functions had returned.

flashcards.front: What happens if an exception is thrown and no matching catch exists anywhere in the call chain?
flashcards.back: std::terminate() is called, which by default calls abort() and ends the program abnormally; a custom handler can be installed with set_terminate().

flashcards.front: How does an exception carry arguments (data) to its handler?
flashcards.back: Throw an object of a class whose constructor stores the data (e.g. throw RangeError(value)); the handler catches it by reference and reads the data through member functions such as what() or get().

questions.explanation: throw 5 leaves the try block at once, so "C" is skipped. The int handler prints 5, and execution then continues after the handler, printing D.
The try block finishes without throwing, so its handlers, even the catch-all, are skipped and execution continues with the statement after them.

questions.questionText: When a catch block finishes normally (without throwing again), where does execution continue?
options: At the statement immediately after the throw that raised the exception
At the beginning of the try block, which is executed again
At the first statement after the last catch block of that try-catch construct
Nowhere: the program always ends once an exception has been handled
questions.explanation: C++ uses the termination model: the code after the throw point is abandoned, and once a handler completes, control passes to the statement following the whole try-catch sequence.

questions.questionText: Which header declares std::runtime_error, std::logic_error and std::out_of_range?
questions.explanation: <stdexcept> holds the standard error classes derived from logic_error and runtime_error. <exception> declares the base class std::exception and functions such as terminate() and set_terminate(), but not these derived error classes.

questions.questionText: What does the virtual member function what() of std::exception return?
options: An int error code identifying the exception
The line number at which the exception was thrown
A C-style string (const char*) describing the exception
A bool telling whether the exception has already been handled
questions.explanation: what() is declared as virtual const char* what() const noexcept; derived classes such as runtime_error return the message that was passed to their constructor.
Handler matching does not apply the usual arithmetic promotions, so the char 'x' is not caught by catch (int). The char handler matches exactly and prints the character itself.

questions.questionText: In standard C++, what does an ordinary new expression such as new int[n] do when it cannot obtain the requested memory?
options: It returns nullptr, which the program must test
It returns a pointer to a zero-sized block
questions.explanation: Ordinary new reports failure by throwing std::bad_alloc (declared in <new>). Only the nothrow form, new (nothrow) T, returns nullptr instead.

questions.questionText: Which class is the common base of all the exception classes thrown by the C++ standard library?
questions.explanation: std::exception is the root of the hierarchy: logic_error, runtime_error, bad_alloc, bad_cast and the others all derive from it, so catch (const exception &e) catches any of them.

questions.questionText: Where must a catch (...) handler be placed among the handlers of a try block?
options: After all the other handlers, as the last one
Anywhere, because the order of handlers does not matter
Only in main(), never inside other functions
questions.explanation: Handlers are tried in the order written and catch (...) matches every exception, so a handler after it could never run; the language therefore requires catch (...) to be the last handler.

options: start is printed, then std::terminate() ends the program abnormally because no handler catches the int
start and end are both printed, because an exception thrown outside a try block is ignored
Nothing is printed: the program does not compile because throw appears outside a try block
start is printed and the program ends normally, returning 1 from main
questions.explanation: throw is legal anywhere, but the search for a handler leaves main without finding one, so std::terminate() is called, which by default calls abort(). endl has already flushed start to the screen.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the type of the object thrown by a throw expression is correct?
options: It must be an object of a class derived from std::exception
It must be an int error code
It can be of almost any type: a built-in type such as int, a pointer such as const char*, or a class object
It must be a string literal describing the error
questions.explanation: throw 5, throw "text" and throw MyError() are all legal. Deriving exception classes from std::exception is only a good convention, because it lets callers catch everything through one base class.

questions.questionText: What must immediately follow a try block in C++?
options: Nothing, because catch handlers are optional
questions.explanation: A try block is always followed directly by at least one catch clause. C++ has no finally keyword; clean-up is done by destructors (RAII) instead.
check(2) prints ok2. check(-3) throws before printing, so the rest of the try block, including check(4), is skipped and the handler prints neg-3.

out_of_range derives from logic_error, and handlers are tested in the order written, so the first handler already matches and only it runs. The out_of_range handler is unreachable; it should have been written first.
catch (Base b) copies only the Base part of the Derived object into b (slicing), so the virtual call gives Base. catch (Base &b) binds to the exception object itself, whose dynamic type is Derived.
b and then a are constructed. The throw unwinds f, destroying a, and then leaves the try block, destroying b; the handler runs only after all these locals have been destroyed.

questions.questionText: Why is catch (const MyError &e) usually preferred to catch (MyError e)?
options: Catching a class type by value is a compile error
A reference handler skips stack unwinding and is therefore faster
Only a reference handler can catch an object of a class derived from MyError
It avoids copying the exception object and avoids slicing, so virtual functions such as what() use the thrown object's real type
questions.explanation: A by-value handler copy-initialises a new MyError from the exception, slicing off any derived part. A reference binds to the exception object itself. Catching by value is legal and does match derived classes, only in sliced form.

options: Nothing is printed; the program terminates
questions.explanation: The literal 2.5 has type double. Handlers do not apply standard conversions such as double to float or double to int, so neither typed handler matches and catch (...) takes the exception.

The string literal is thrown as a const char*, which the inner catch (int) cannot take, so the exception leaves the inner try-catch and "after " is skipped as well. The outer handler receives the pointer and prints outer oops.

An exception thrown inside a handler is not caught by the other handlers of the same try block; the search starts from the enclosing try. So the inner int handler prints A and the outer double handler prints C.

questions.questionText: What happens if the statement throw; (with no operand) is executed when no exception is currently being handled?
options: The code fails to compile, because throw; is allowed only inside a catch block
The most recently handled exception is thrown again
questions.explanation: throw; rethrows the exception currently being handled. It is syntactically legal anywhere, but if no exception is being handled when it runs, the program calls std::terminate().

options: Nothing is printed, because catch (const exception &) does not match a MyErr
The program does not compile, because what() cannot be overridden
questions.explanation: MyErr derives publicly from std::exception, so the base-class reference handler catches it, and because what() is virtual the call reaches MyErr::what().

The noexcept operator is evaluated at compile time from the declarations only: a() is declared noexcept (true, 1), b() has no specification and so may throw (false, 0), and noexcept(false) states explicitly that c() may throw (0).

options: std::terminate() is called, so neither caught nor end is printed
It does not compile, because a noexcept function cannot contain a throw
questions.explanation: An exception that tries to leave a noexcept function makes the program call std::terminate() at once; it never reaches the caller's handler. The code compiles (a compiler may only warn).
f(3) does not throw and returns 3. In f(8), throw 8 passes the value to the handler parameter v, and the handler's return statement returns -8 to main.

questions.questionText: Which of these situations does NOT lead to std::terminate() being called?
options: An exception that escapes from a function declared noexcept
An exception that propagates out of main() with no matching handler
A destructor that throws while the stack is being unwound for another exception
An exception that is caught by a catch (...) handler in main()
questions.explanation: catch (...) matches every exception, so the program simply continues after that handler. The other three are the classic causes of terminate(): an exception leaving a noexcept function, no handler at all, and a second exception during unwinding.

questions.questionText: std::out_of_range, which vector::at() throws for a bad index, is derived directly from which class?
questions.explanation: out_of_range is a logic_error (the mistake could in principle be detected before running the program), alongside invalid_argument, domain_error and length_error. range_error is a runtime_error meant for arithmetic results out of range.

runtime_error is not derived from logic_error, so the first handler is skipped. The second binds a reference to the runtime_error object, and the virtual what() returns the message passed to its constructor.
v has valid indices 0 to 2, so three assignments succeed and n becomes 3. For i = 3, at() throws before n++ runs, and the handler adds 10, giving 13; v[2] was set to 2.

questions.questionText: Under C++17, what happens to a declaration such as void f() throw(int); ?
options: It compiles, and any exception thrown by f is converted to int
It is ill-formed: dynamic exception specifications were removed in C++17, and noexcept is used instead
It compiles, and throwing any type other than int calls std::unexpected()
It compiles, and the compiler checks the body of f to make sure it throws only int
questions.explanation: throw(type-list) specifications were deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17, so a C++17 compiler rejects them. In C++03 a violation called std::unexpected(); today a function states only whether it can throw, using noexcept.

questions.questionText: Under the C++03 standard, a function declared as void g() throw(int) threw a double. What did the run-time system do?
options: It converted the double to int so that the caller could catch it
It let the double propagate to the caller, because the specification was only documentation
It called std::unexpected(), whose default behaviour is to call std::terminate()
Nothing: such code was rejected at compile time
questions.explanation: A dynamic exception specification was enforced at run time: throwing an unlisted type called unexpected(), whose default handler calls terminate(). set_unexpected() could install a replacement handler, for example one that throws an allowed type.

No handler matches the double, so std::terminate() calls the handler installed with set_terminate(). It prints custom and ends the program with exit(0), which flushes the output; a terminate handler must end the program rather than return.

questions.questionText: Inside a catch (...) handler, how can the program make use of the exception that was caught?
options: Through an implicit variable named e
By calling what() directly, since every exception has it
Through the this pointer of the handler
It cannot name the object, but it can rethrow it unchanged with throw;
questions.explanation: catch (...) has no parameter, so the object is not accessible by name (and it may not even be a class type with what()). The usual pattern is local clean-up followed by throw; to pass the same exception on to an outer handler.

options: The delete[] is skipped, so the array leaks; holding it in a vector<int> or unique_ptr<int[]> fixes this
Stack unwinding calls delete[] on buf automatically
The program always terminates, because process() has no try block
Nothing, because the memory is released as soon as process() is left
questions.explanation: Unwinding destroys local objects, but buf is a raw pointer and destroying a pointer does not free what it points to. RAII types such as vector or unique_ptr free the memory in their destructors, which do run during unwinding.

options: Nothing is printed; the program terminates
questions.explanation: A thrown string literal decays to const char*. Handlers never apply user-defined conversions such as the string constructor, so catch (const string &) is skipped and the pointer handler prints abc.

divide(7, 2) uses integer division and returns 3. divide(9, 0) throws a DivError built from its arguments, nothing more is printed from the try block, and the handler reads the stored values back, printing 9/0.
For m = 0, throw e creates a new exception by copying e, and the copy has e's static type B (the D part is sliced off). For m = 1, throw; rethrows the original D object, so the virtual call prints D.
Odd i are added normally: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9. Even i throw an Err carrying i × 10, and the handler adds 20 + 40 = 60 instead; the try is inside the loop, so the loop continues. Total 9 + 60 = 69.

Member m is constructed before the body of X's constructor runs. The body throws, so x is never fully constructed and ~X() is not called, but the already constructed member m is destroyed before the handler runs.

The throw in c() unwinds c and b, destroying their locals (printing c, then b) and skipping "B". The handler in a() prints h, a() continues with A, its local g prints a when a() returns, and finally main prints M.

k = 0 throws an A, which only catch (A &) matches. k = 1 throws a B: catch (C &) does not match, but catch (A &) does because B is derived from A, so the later B handler is never reached. k = 2 throws a C, caught by the first handler.

y is destroyed as the throw leaves the inner try (2), then f's handler prints c and rethrows. The rethrow unwinds f, destroying x (1), then leaves main's try block, destroying z (3), and main's handler prints m.

rec(4), rec(3), rec(2), rec(1) and rec(0) are all active when the throw happens, each with its own D object: 5 objects. Stack unwinding destroys all five before the handler in main runs, so dtors is 5.

The inner handler catches through a reference to the base runtime_error, prints the message and rethrows with throw;, which passes on the original AppError object. The outer AppError handler therefore matches and prints its code, 404.

The exception thrown in level(0) is caught in turn by the handlers of level(0), level(1) and level(2); each doubles the same object through the reference and rethrows it with throw;. So hits = 3 and the value is 1 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 when main catches it.
